theme: Unit 2 review, Common Grace & the Noahic Covenant
memoryText: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and reflection on what you have learned in Unit 2.

Begin by memorizing the verse above if you have not already. Genesis 6:8 is the hinge of the entire Noah narrative. Surrounding this single sentence is the bleakest assessment of humanity in the Old Testament (verse 5: “every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually”) and the announcement of the coming flood (verse 7). But in the middle of judgment, this one verse stands out: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.”

This is the first occurrence of the Hebrew word hen, favor, or grace, in the Bible. Everything that the New Testament will say about salvation by grace is anticipated here. Noah did not earn favor. He did not negotiate for favor. He found it. Grace, by definition, is what is found, not what is achieved.

Say this verse aloud several times today. Notice the conjunction: “But Noah found favor.” That “but” is everything. In a world of judgment, there is a “but.” In a heart of rebellion, there is a “but.” That “but” is the difference between being lost with the world and being preserved by grace. The same “but” applies to every believer in Christ, in a world that is, in the language of Romans 1, under the wrath of God, there is a “but” for those who have found favor through faith in Jesus. “But God, being rich in mercy…” (Ephesians 2:4). The story of salvation always turns on that small word.
unitRecap:
In Unit 2 you have traveled through Genesis 4 to 11, the early chapters of humanity after the Fall. The unit began with Cain’s murder of Abel, the first violence in human history, and the warning that “sin is crouching at the door.” It then moved through the genealogy of Adam to Noah, where ten generations were punctuated by the repeated phrase “and he died”, except for Enoch, who walked with God and was not. The pre-flood corruption of humanity was so total that God resolved to start over, but Noah found favor.

The flood narrative was one of the longer readings of the unit: judgment by water, the ark as a microcosm of creation, the de-creation and re-creation of the world, the great hinge of “God remembered Noah.” Then came the Noahic Covenant, God’s pledge to preserve creation, including “man and beast,” under the sign of the rainbow. This is the foundation of common grace.

The unit’s final reading was Genesis 10-11: the Table of Nations showing how the post-flood world filled up, and the tower of Babel showing how quickly human pride re-asserted itself. Humanity tried to make a name for itself; God scattered them. But the chapter ended with the line of Shem narrowing down to Terah and Abram, setting up Unit 3.

The Psalms then taught us how to respond to all of this. Psalm 36 lifted our eyes to God’s steadfast love that reaches to the heavens, bigger than every wickedness we had witnessed. Psalm 33 reminded us that God brings the counsel of the nations to nothing while his own counsel stands forever. And Psalm 9 sang the justice of God who hears the cry of the oppressed and reigns from a throne of judgment.

The big theological lessons of this unit are these: Sin spreads from generation to generation, but the line of promise is preserved. Judgment is real and is sometimes severe, but it is always paired with mercy for the faithful. The Noahic Covenant is God’s commitment to maintain the world as a stage on which redemption can unfold. Common grace touches every life and every culture, regardless of belief. And underneath every story of rebellion, God is patiently moving toward Abram, through whom blessing will eventually come to all the families of the earth.

reviewQuestions.question: How does the story of Cain and Abel show the nature and spread of sin?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Revisit Genesis 4. Sin is shown crouching at the door, an active force seeking to consume. Cain refuses to rule over it, and the result is the first murder. Notice how quickly sin escalates: by Lamech (verses 23-24), the cycle of vengeance has multiplied seventy-sevenfold. Sin is not just an individual failure; it is a multiplying force that ruptures families, communities, and generations. Write a few sentences in your own words about what Genesis 4 teaches you about how sin works.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the Noahic covenant, and who does it include?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Read Genesis 9:8-17 again. The Noahic Covenant is God’s promise never again to destroy the earth by flood. Notice its scope: it is made with Noah and his descendants, but also with “every living creature” on the earth. This is the most universal of God’s covenants. It is also the foundation of common grace, every harvest, every season, every birth in every culture is a gift under this covenant. What does it tell you about God that he extends this covenant to all of creation, even to people who do not believe in him?

reviewQuestions.question: What does the tower of Babel reveal about human nature and God’s purposes?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at Genesis 11:1-9. Humans gathered together to “make a name for ourselves” and to build a tower “with its top in the heavens.” Three sins converge in this story: pride (making a name), idolatry (replacing God’s name with their own), and disobedience (gathering rather than filling the earth). God’s response, confusion of language and scattering, is judgment, but also redemption strategy. Through scattering, God sets up the long story by which the gospel will eventually reach every nation. The reversal begins at Pentecost. How does this shape the way you see the world today?

reviewQuestions.question: How does common grace differ from saving grace?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Common grace is the kindness God extends to all humanity, regardless of belief, the rain that falls on the just and the unjust, the harvests, the seasons, the beauty in human cultures, the goodness in human relationships. It is grounded in the Noahic Covenant. Saving grace is the particular grace by which God redeems his elect through Christ, the grace by which Noah found favor in God’s eyes, and by which every believer is brought into the family of God. Both are gifts. Both are unearned. But common grace preserves the world; saving grace transforms hearts. Sit with the distinction. How does understanding the difference help you appreciate both the beauty in the unbelieving world and the particular wonder of your own salvation?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for his patience with the world and with you, in your own words.
Thank him for the line of promise that leads to Christ.
Ask him to keep what you learned in this unit alive in how you live.
